questions.question: What is "general AI" (or "strong AI"), in contrast to narrow AI?

options.A: An AI system that has been certified against an official quality standard
options.B: A hypothetical AI with human-like ability to perform any intellectual task, not yet achieved
options.C: An AI system that runs on multiple GPUs at the same time for extra speed
options.D: An AI system that has been trained on a very large number of different data sets

questions.explanation: General AI refers to a hypothetical system with broad, human-like intelligence across many domains, unlike narrow AI which performs one specific task. It remains a research goal rather than a deployed reality.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes an "AI-based system"?

options.A: A system that only performs simple, fixed, rule-based calculations
options.B: A system that has no user interface and runs entirely in the background
options.C: A system with one or more components shaped by an ML model
options.D: Any software system that was written using a modern programming language

questions.explanation: An AI-based system incorporates AI components, typically ML models, that shape its behavior, which distinguishes it from purely conventionally coded software.

questions.question: Which of these is a commonly cited example of an AI application area?

options.A: Version control, used for tracking changes to source code files
options.B: Computer vision, used for tasks such as recognizing objects in images
options.C: Load balancing, used for distributing network traffic across servers
options.D: Database indexing, used for speeding up query lookups

questions.explanation: Computer vision is a well-known AI application area. The other options describe conventional software engineering concerns unrelated to AI.

questions.question: Why do many AI-based systems exhibit "non-determinism," where the same input can produce different outputs on different runs?

options.A: Every AI-based system is fully deterministic and never varies its output
options.B: AI-based systems are required by law to vary their answers between runs
options.C: Random init, sampling or parallel execution can cause variation
options.D: Non-determinism only ever occurs due to a defect in the underlying hardware

questions.explanation: Sources such as random seeds, sampling strategies in generation, or non-deterministic parallel execution can cause the same input to yield different outputs, which complicates testing and defect reproduction.

questions.question: What motivates risk-tiered regulation of AI systems, such as the approach taken by the EU AI Act?

options.A: Requiring that all AI systems be open source before they can be used
options.B: Applying stricter obligations to AI uses that pose greater potential harm to people or society
options.C: Banning all forms of AI development within the regulated jurisdiction
options.D: Applying identical rules to every AI system regardless of its purpose or potential harm

questions.explanation: Risk tiering concentrates regulatory obligations, such as testing, documentation and oversight, on higher-risk uses like biometric identification or credit scoring, while lighter-touch rules apply to lower-risk uses.

questions.question: What does it mean for an AI system to be described as "self-learning" or "adaptive," as opposed to a "locked" system?

options.A: Its behavior can continue to change after deployment as it learns from new data
options.B: Its parameters are permanently fixed once it is deployed to production
options.C: It requires no training data of any kind before it can be used
options.D: It cannot be tested at all under any circumstances

questions.explanation: A self-learning system keeps updating based on new data after deployment, in contrast to a locked model whose parameters are frozen, which has significant implications for how and how often it must be tested.

questions.question: Why is specialized hardware, such as GPUs or TPUs, commonly used for training and running many AI models?

options.A: Ordinary CPUs are physically incapable of performing any arithmetic operations
options.B: Specialized hardware is legally required for any AI system regardless of its size
options.C: They accelerate the massive parallel numerical computation involved
options.D: Specialized hardware eliminates the need to test the resulting AI system

questions.explanation: Training and running many machine learning models, especially deep neural networks, involves large-scale matrix and vector computation that GPUs and TPUs are architecturally optimized to accelerate.

questions.question: What is the "AI effect," a phenomenon sometimes discussed when describing the history of AI?

options.A: The physical effect of AI hardware overheating during prolonged training runs
options.B: The tendency to stop calling a capability "AI" once it becomes routine and well understood
options.C: The legal effect of a regulation once it comes fully into force
options.D: The financial effect of an AI project on a company's quarterly earnings

questions.explanation: The AI effect describes how tasks once considered signs of intelligence, such as chess-playing programs, are often reclassified as "just computation" once they become commonplace, shifting the perceived boundary of what counts as AI.

questions.question: What distinguishes generative AI from a discriminative AI model?

options.A: Generative AI never requires any training data, while discriminative AI always does
options.B: Generative AI is always smaller in size than any discriminative model ever built
options.C: Generative AI creates new content, while discriminative AI classifies or scores existing input
options.D: Generative AI can only process numeric input, while discriminative AI only processes text

questions.explanation: Generative models learn to produce new, original outputs, such as text or images, whereas discriminative models learn to distinguish between or label existing inputs, which is the core functional difference.

questions.question: Which AI-specific quality characteristic concerns whether a system's outputs remain acceptable when inputs are noisy or slightly perturbed?

options.A: Robustness
options.B: Maintainability
options.C: Installability
options.D: Portability

questions.explanation: Robustness describes tolerance to noisy, unusual or adversarially perturbed input, a concern that is especially prominent for AI-based systems compared with conventional quality characteristics.

questions.question: What does "functional adaptability" mean as a quality characteristic for AI-based systems?

options.A: The system's ability to be translated into different spoken languages
options.B: The system's ability to be installed on different types of hardware
options.C: The system's ability to adjust its behavior as it learns from new data over time
options.D: The system's ability to run without consuming any electrical power

questions.explanation: Functional adaptability captures how well a self-learning system can update its behavior in response to new data, which is a benefit for staying current but also a distinct testing challenge.

questions.question: Why is "transparency" considered important for many AI-based systems?

options.A: Stakeholders often need to understand what data and factors influenced a given output
options.B: Transparency means the source code must always be published publicly
options.C: Transparency guarantees that a system will never make an incorrect prediction
options.D: Transparency is only relevant to systems that have no users at all

questions.explanation: Transparency concerns the visibility of what informs a system's decisions, which supports trust, accountability and effective oversight, especially for consequential decisions.

questions.question: Which quality characteristic specifically addresses a human's ability to intervene and override or stop an AI system's actions?

options.A: Compatibility
options.B: Time behavior under normal load
options.C: Autonomy / human oversight
options.D: Reliability of installation

questions.explanation: Autonomy-related characteristics cover the degree of independent action an AI system takes and the corresponding ability of a human to intervene, override or halt it, which matters greatly for safety-critical uses.

questions.question: What does "explainability" of an AI-based system primarily concern?

options.A: Making the reasoning behind an output understandable
options.B: The physical size of the file containing the trained model
options.C: The number of programming languages used to build the system
options.D: The speed at which the system produces its outputs for a user

questions.explanation: Explainability is about making the reasoning behind an output understandable to relevant stakeholders, which can range from a full mechanistic account to simplified, human-friendly justifications.

questions.question: Which AI-specific standard extends the general ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model to address characteristics relevant to AI systems?

options.A: ISO/IEC 25059
options.B: IEEE 802.11
options.C: ISO/IEC 27001
options.D: ISO 9001

questions.explanation: ISO/IEC 25059 builds on the ISO/IEC 25010 quality model to specifically address AI system quality characteristics, such as those introduced in this domain.

questions.question: Which quality characteristic concerns whether an AI-based system continues to operate correctly as underlying data distributions or operating conditions change?

options.A: Portability, since it only concerns moving the system between operating systems
options.B: Installability, since it only concerns how easily the system can be set up
options.C: Co-existence, since it only concerns running alongside other unrelated software
options.D: Adaptability, since it must keep performing despite shifting conditions

questions.explanation: Adaptability specifically addresses continued acceptable behavior as the environment or data distribution shifts, which is a distinct concern from installation or coexistence-related characteristics.

questions.question: In supervised learning, what does the training data typically consist of?

options.A: Only input examples, with no output information provided at all
options.B: A single example that the entire model is built to memorize
options.C: Input examples paired with their correct, known output labels
options.D: A fixed set of hand-written rules describing correct behavior

questions.explanation: Supervised learning uses labeled examples, pairs of inputs and their correct outputs, from which the model learns to generalize to new, unseen inputs.

questions.question: Which ML task groups similar data points together without using any predefined category labels?

options.A: Classification
options.B: Supervised fine-tuning
options.C: Clustering
options.D: Regression

questions.explanation: Clustering is an unsupervised task that discovers natural groupings in data on its own, unlike classification and regression, which both require labeled examples to learn from.

questions.question: Why is a model's final performance normally reported using a held-out test set rather than the validation set used for tuning?

options.A: So it gives a less biased estimate than the tuning-influenced validation set
options.B: Reporting on the validation set always produces a lower score than the test set would
options.C: The validation set is always mathematically identical to the test set in every project
options.D: Test sets are only required for models that will never be deployed to production

questions.explanation: Because the validation set influenced choices like hyperparameters, evaluating on it can be optimistic; a completely untouched test set gives a fairer final estimate.

questions.question: Overfitting occurs when a model does which of the following?

options.A: Fails to learn any meaningful pattern from the training data at all
options.B: Fits both the training data and new data equally well and accurately
options.C: Fits the training data very closely but generalizes poorly to new, unseen data
options.D: Requires no training data whatsoever to produce useful predictions

questions.explanation: Overfitting means the model has essentially memorized quirks of the training set rather than learning generalizable patterns, so it performs worse on new data.

questions.question: Underfitting is indicated when a model shows which pattern?

options.A: Performance that improves indefinitely the longer training continues
options.B: Poor performance on both the training data and new, unseen data
options.C: Excellent performance on training data but poor performance on new data
options.D: Excellent performance on both training data and new data

questions.explanation: Underfitting means the model has not learned enough of the underlying pattern, so it performs poorly even on the data it was trained on, unlike overfitting where training performance is good but generalization is poor.

questions.question: Why does changing a hyperparameter, such as the number of training epochs, typically require re-running the training process?

options.A: Hyperparameters have no influence at all on the resulting trained model
options.B: Hyperparameters are set before training and shape how the model's learned parameters are derived
options.C: Hyperparameters are themselves learned automatically and update continuously during training
options.D: Changing a hyperparameter always corrupts the training data permanently

questions.explanation: Because hyperparameters configure the training process itself, changing one means the learned parameters that depend on that process need to be derived again.

questions.question: Which of these scenarios is best suited to an unsupervised, rather than supervised, learning approach?

options.A: Predicting a house's sale price using past sales with known, recorded prices
options.B: Predicting whether an email is spam using thousands of emails already labeled spam or not spam
options.C: Classifying X-ray images as showing a fracture or not, using images labeled by radiologists
options.D: Grouping customers into segments when no one has labeled which segment each customer belongs to

questions.explanation: With no existing labels for customer segments, the task fits unsupervised learning's strength of discovering structure on its own, unlike the other scenarios which all have labeled ground truth available.

questions.question: What does "transfer learning" involve?

options.A: Reusing a model trained on one task as a starting point for a related task
options.B: Physically moving a trained model file from one server to another
options.C: Transferring ownership of a dataset from one company to another
options.D: Training a brand-new model completely from scratch every single time

questions.explanation: Transfer learning leverages knowledge already captured in a model trained for one task to speed up or improve learning on a related task, often needing much less new data.

questions.question: What does a confusion matrix show for a classification model?

options.A: The number of employees who contributed to labeling the training data
options.B: Correct and incorrect prediction counts by actual versus predicted class
options.C: The physical memory usage of the model while it is running
options.D: The exact source code used to implement the classification algorithm

questions.explanation: A confusion matrix cross-tabulates actual versus predicted classes, revealing not just overall accuracy but the specific types of errors, such as false positives and false negatives.

questions.question: What does recall (sensitivity) of a classifier measure?

options.A: The overall proportion of all predictions, positive or negative, that are correct
options.B: The proportion of actual positive cases that the model correctly identifies
options.C: The proportion of predicted positive cases that are actually positive
options.D: The total number of features used as input to the model

questions.explanation: Recall focuses on how many of the real positive cases were caught by the model, which matters most when missing a positive case, such as a disease or fraud case, is costly.

questions.question: What does precision measure for a classifier?

options.A: The proportion of all predictions, whether positive or negative, that are correct
options.B: The proportion of predicted positive cases that are actually positive
options.C: The average time taken by the model to produce a single prediction
options.D: The proportion of actual positive cases that the model correctly identifies

questions.explanation: Precision measures how trustworthy a positive prediction is, which matters most when a false positive, such as wrongly flagging a legitimate transaction as fraud, is costly.

questions.question: A fraud-detection model that always predicts "not fraud" scores 99% accuracy, since fraud is rare. What does this illustrate?

options.A: Accuracy is meaningless and should never be reported for any classification model
options.B: A single aggregate metric like accuracy can hide complete failure to detect the rare, important class
options.C: A 99% accuracy score is impossible unless the model has genuinely learned to detect fraud
options.D: The model must actually be excellent at detecting fraud, since its accuracy is very high

questions.explanation: On imbalanced data, a trivial always-predict-majority model still scores high on accuracy while being useless for the task, which is exactly why metrics like recall matter for the rare class.

questions.question: What does "feature engineering" refer to in the ML development workflow?

options.A: Deciding which programming language the final application will be written in
options.B: Selecting, transforming or creating input variables to improve model performance
options.C: Physically assembling the hardware servers that will run the trained model
options.D: Writing the legal license agreement that accompanies a data set

questions.explanation: Feature engineering shapes the raw data into more informative inputs for the model, which can significantly affect how well the model learns and performs.

questions.question: What is the "test oracle problem" for many AI-based systems?

options.A: The oracle problem only affects systems that produce numeric outputs
options.B: It is often difficult to know the definitively correct expected output for a given input
options.C: AI-based systems can never be tested using any oracle of any kind
options.D: Test oracles are only relevant to systems that have no machine learning components

questions.explanation: For tasks like image captioning or sentiment analysis, there may be no single definitively "correct" answer, which makes deciding pass or fail harder than for deterministic conventional software.

questions.question: A metamorphic relation for a translation model states "translating a sentence and then translating it back should preserve its approximate meaning." What is being applied here?

options.A: Back-to-back testing, which always compares two entirely separate, independently built systems
options.B: A/B testing, which always requires routing a portion of live user traffic
options.C: Neuron coverage analysis, which is specific to inspecting internal network activations
options.D: Metamorphic testing, checking a relation rather than a fixed result

questions.explanation: This is a metamorphic relation, a property that should hold between an input and a transformed input, letting testers check correctness without knowing one precise expected translation.

questions.question: What is an "adversarial example" in the context of testing an AI model?

options.A: An input randomly selected from the original, unmodified training data set
options.B: An input that is always guaranteed to be classified correctly by any model
options.C: A test case that only checks the user interface of the application
options.D: An input crafted, often subtly, to cause an incorrect prediction

questions.explanation: Adversarial examples exploit a model's weaknesses with carefully crafted, often imperceptible, perturbations, revealing robustness gaps that regular testing might miss.

questions.question: What does "red teaming" a generative AI system typically involve?

options.A: Measuring how quickly the system responds to a simple, single test prompt
options.B: Reviewing only the visual design and color scheme of the system's user interface
options.C: Deliberately probing the system with adversarial or harmful prompts to find weaknesses
options.D: Verifying that the system's source code compiles without any errors

questions.explanation: Red teaming actively attempts to elicit unsafe, biased or otherwise undesirable outputs, which is a key technique for assessing the safety of generative AI systems before release.

questions.question: A tester with no predefined script freely tries unusual prompts against a chatbot to see if anything surprising happens. What testing approach is this?

options.A: Back-to-back testing, which always compares two separate model implementations
options.B: Statistical testing, which always requires a large, predefined sample of inputs
options.C: Neuron coverage testing, which always inspects the network's internal activations
options.D: Exploratory testing, which relies on tester judgment and investigation rather than a fixed script

questions.explanation: Investigating freely without a predetermined script, guided by the tester's own judgment and curiosity, is the defining characteristic of exploratory testing.

questions.question: Why is a "locked" ML model generally easier to test than a self-learning one?

options.A: Locked models cannot process any new, previously unseen input data
options.B: Locked models are always smaller in size than self-learning models
options.C: Locked models never need to be tested at all under any circumstances
options.D: Its behavior stays fixed, so results stay valid until it's retrained

questions.explanation: Because a locked model's parameters do not change after deployment, tests run against it stay valid over time, unlike a continuously adapting model whose behavior can drift.

questions.question: What is a "pseudo-oracle" approach to testing an AI-based system?

options.A: Skipping the need for any expected result entirely for every test case
options.B: Randomly guessing at the expected output for each individual test case
options.C: Using an independently developed alternative implementation to compare outputs
options.D: Using the exact same model under test as its own source of expected results

questions.explanation: A pseudo-oracle, such as an independently built alternative model or implementation, provides a point of comparison when no ground truth is available, helping to flag suspicious discrepancies.

questions.question: What does "automation bias" refer to during testing or use of an AI-based system?

options.A: A legal requirement that automated tests must always be preferred over manual ones
options.B: A statistical bias that is only found in the mathematics of neural networks
options.C: A hardware limitation specific to GPU-accelerated automated testing tools
options.D: The tendency of people to over-trust an automated system's output without sufficient scrutiny

questions.explanation: Automation bias describes over-reliance on a system's automated output, which can cause testers or users to miss errors that a more skeptical review would catch.

questions.question: A team checks that a data pipeline correctly cleans and encodes records before any model is trained on them. Which ML-specific test level does this belong to?

options.A: ML development testing, since it concerns build pipelines and code checks only
options.B: Input data testing
options.C: Model testing, since it concerns evaluating a trained model directly
options.D: Standard system testing of a conventional, non-AI application

questions.explanation: Checking data quality and preparation before training falls under input data testing, distinct from model testing, which evaluates the trained model, and development testing, which covers code and pipelines more broadly.

questions.question: Why should testers ideally be involved early in an AI project, such as during requirements and data planning?

options.A: Early involvement catches data and testability risks before they're costly
options.B: Testers are legally required to approve every line of code before it is written
options.C: Early involvement guarantees the resulting model will always achieve perfect accuracy
options.D: Testers are the only people qualified to select which programming language to use

questions.explanation: Issues found early, such as unclear requirements or foreseeable data quality problems, are typically far cheaper to address than the same issues discovered after a model has already been built.

questions.question: What kind of information does statistical testing of an AI-based system's performance typically report, beyond a single point value?

options.A: The number of unrelated meetings held during the project's timeline
options.B: Only the exact line number in the source code where each defect exists
options.C: A measure of uncertainty, such as a confidence interval, around the reported metric
options.D: The physical color of the servers running the AI model

questions.explanation: Because measured performance can vary with the sample of data used, statistical testing often reports a confidence interval or similar uncertainty measure alongside the point estimate, giving a fuller picture of reliability.

questions.question: What might a "partial oracle" check when a full, precise expected output is not available?

options.A: A checkable property, like format or a known constraint
options.B: The complete, exact correctness of every single detail of the output
options.C: Nothing at all, since a partial oracle can never verify any property of an output
options.D: Only whether the system crashed during execution, and nothing else

questions.explanation: A partial oracle verifies something checkable, like output range, format or a known invariant, even when the full correct answer cannot be determined, offering partial confidence.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: A saying in machine learning is "garbage in, garbage out." What does this most directly warn testers about?

options.A: Poor-quality training data tends to produce a poor-quality trained model, whatever the algorithm
options.B: Data quality issues can only ever appear after a model has already been deployed
options.C: Poorly written code can never affect a model regardless of the data used to train it
options.D: A model's hardware, not its data, is always the dominant factor in its final quality

questions.explanation: The saying captures that an ML model's behavior is learned from its data, so data flaws tend to surface directly as model flaws, which is why input data testing matters so much.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: What does "data representativeness" mean for a training or test dataset?

options.A: The dataset has been reviewed and approved by a company's legal department
options.B: The dataset reflects the real-world distribution of cases the system will encounter
options.C: The dataset is stored using a widely supported, standard file format
options.D: The dataset contains only positive examples and no negative examples at all

questions.explanation: A representative dataset mirrors the actual population and conditions the deployed system will face, so the model's learned behavior generalizes well to real usage.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: What does "label noise" refer to in a training dataset?

options.A: Background audio noise that is present in an audio training dataset
options.B: A feature value that has already been correctly scaled and normalized
options.C: Incorrect or inconsistent labels assigned to some of the training examples
options.D: The total number of distinct labels used across the whole dataset

questions.explanation: Label noise describes mistakes or inconsistencies in the ground-truth labels themselves, which can mislead the model during training and degrade its eventual accuracy.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: Which of these is an inconsistent-formatting issue that input data testing might flag in a dataset?

options.A: A GPU cluster configured to train several models at the same time
options.B: A data center located in a Region with lower electricity costs
options.C: A training script written in a widely used, well-documented programming language
options.D: A date field stored as "2026-01-05" in some rows and "01/05/2026" in others

questions.explanation: Mixed date formats within the same field are a concrete formatting inconsistency that input data testing looks for, since it can confuse parsing and produce incorrect derived features.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: A team accidentally trains a model on a data file that includes rows later used for testing. What is the most likely consequence?

options.A: The model will be unable to produce any output at all once this mistake happens
options.B: The mistake has no effect on reported metrics, since ML models cannot memorize data
options.C: Reported test performance will look better than the model's real-world performance actually is
options.D: Test performance will always become worse than the model's real-world performance

questions.explanation: Data leakage of this kind lets the model effectively memorize the test examples, inflating reported metrics beyond what the model would actually achieve on genuinely new data.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: A team has too few example images of a rare product defect to train a reliable classifier. Flipping, rotating and slightly recoloring the existing images to create more training examples is an application of what technique?

options.A: Cross-validation
options.B: Data augmentation
options.C: Feature engineering
options.D: Data drift correction

questions.explanation: Creating modified variants of existing examples to enlarge a training set is data augmentation, which is especially useful when genuinely new examples of a rare case are hard to obtain.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: What does "data drift" mean for a deployed ML system?

options.A: The programming language used to build the model changes after deployment
options.B: The physical storage location of a dataset changes from one server to another
options.C: The number of employees on the data science team increases over time
options.D: Production data's statistical properties shift from what it was trained on

questions.explanation: Data drift occurs when the distribution of real-world input data shifts away from what the model was trained on, which can silently degrade the model's accuracy in production.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: A hiring model is trained mostly on resumes of people previously hired by the company, when past hiring itself favored certain groups. What kind of bias risk does this illustrate?

options.A: Historical bias, where the training data reflects and can perpetuate a past pattern of unfair outcomes
options.B: Data drift, which only concerns changes in data after the model is already deployed
options.C: Label noise, which only concerns inconsistent or incorrect labels, not who was included
options.D: Overfitting, which only concerns a model fitting its training data too closely

questions.explanation: When historical outcomes embedded in the data reflect past unfairness, training on that data can carry the same pattern forward into the model's predictions, which is historical bias.

questions.question: Why might a tester track how much of a neural network's internal activation space a test suite has exercised?

options.A: To give an AI-specific analogue to code coverage of internal behavior
options.B: Because doing so directly and automatically improves the model's real-world accuracy
options.C: Because this measurement is required before any model can legally be deployed
options.D: Because internal activations always correspond one-to-one with lines of source code

questions.explanation: Neuron coverage adapts the idea of code coverage to a neural network's internal structure, giving some indication of how much of the model's internal behavior a test suite actually exercised.

questions.question: What does back-to-back testing of an ML model typically compare?

options.A: The model's training time against the time taken by an unrelated conventional program
options.B: The number of GPUs used in training against the number used in production
options.C: The new model's outputs against those of a previous, trusted version or implementation
options.D: The model's file size against the file size of the original training dataset

questions.explanation: Back-to-back testing runs the same inputs through two versions or implementations and compares outputs, which helps detect unintended behavioral differences introduced by a change.

questions.question: A recommendation team splits real users into two groups, each seeing a different model version, and compares which group buys more. What testing approach is this?

options.A: Metamorphic testing, which checks output relationships rather than business outcomes
options.B: A/B testing
options.C: Neuron coverage testing, which inspects internal network activations only
options.D: Shadow testing, which never actually shows a new model's results to real users

questions.explanation: Splitting real traffic between two live versions and comparing a real outcome metric is the defining feature of A/B testing, as opposed to shadow testing, where users never see the new model's output.

questions.question: What does "shadow testing" (or a dark launch) of a new model involve?

options.A: The new model runs on real traffic without affecting user-facing results
options.B: Testing the new model only in a completely dark, unlit physical office building
options.C: Deleting the currently deployed model before the new one has been fully tested
options.D: Publishing detailed marketing materials about the new model before it launches

questions.explanation: In shadow testing, the new model processes real production requests in parallel, and its outputs are logged and compared, but users only see the incumbent model's results, limiting risk.

questions.question: How does canary releasing of a new ML model help reduce deployment risk?

options.A: By replacing the new model's outputs with random values for early observers
options.B: By permanently disabling monitoring during the entire deployment process
options.C: By requiring every single user to manually approve the new model before use
options.D: By exposing the new model to a small fraction of real traffic before a full rollout

questions.explanation: A canary release limits exposure to a small slice of real users first, so problems can be caught and the rollout halted before affecting the entire user base.

questions.question: A model predicts house prices, and a tester wants a metric that expresses the typical dollar-amount error between predicted and actual prices. Which metric family is appropriate?

options.A: The F1-score, which combines precision and recall for a classification task
options.B: Precision and recall, which are defined for classification, not for numeric prediction
options.C: A confusion matrix, which tabulates discrete predicted versus actual classes
options.D: Error metrics such as mean absolute error, suited to a regression task

questions.explanation: Predicting a continuous price is a regression task, so error-based metrics like mean absolute error, which express the typical size of the numeric error, are the appropriate choice, not classification metrics.

questions.question: What does verifying the "reproducibility" of an ML training pipeline check?

options.A: That the pipeline never requires any configuration settings to be specified
options.B: That the pipeline's source code is written in more than one programming language
options.C: That the pipeline can only ever be run on one single specific physical machine
options.D: That re-running the pipeline with the same inputs and settings produces consistent results

questions.explanation: Reproducibility testing confirms that given the same data, code and configuration, the training process yields the same or acceptably similar results, which supports trust and debuggability.

questions.question: Why is it important to run automated checks, such as a continuous integration pipeline, on an ML project's training code?

options.A: Because CI pipelines are only relevant to conventional software with no ML component
options.B: Because automated checks remove the need for any model testing after training
options.C: Because continuous integration guarantees the resulting trained model will be perfectly accurate
options.D: To catch regressions in code, data handling or pipeline behavior early, before they reach production

questions.explanation: Just as with conventional software, automated checks on ML code and pipelines catch problems, such as broken preprocessing or a failing training step, quickly and consistently.

questions.question: What is a common example of a check performed as part of ML development testing before a full training run?

options.A: Verifying that all data scientists on the team have the same favorite programming language
options.B: Verifying that the data pipeline runs without errors and outputs correctly shaped data
options.C: Verifying that the training server's case has been physically cleaned
options.D: Verifying that the final deployed model's user interface uses an approved font

questions.explanation: Checking the data pipeline's basic functioning and output shape before a costly full training run helps catch cheap-to-fix problems early, avoiding wasted compute time.

questions.question: Why might a team version both the code and the data used to train a model, not just the code alone?

options.A: Because data never changes over the life of a project, so versioning it is purely symbolic
options.B: Because regulations forbid any project from ever storing more than one version of a dataset
options.C: Because versioning data automatically makes model training run measurably faster
options.D: So that a specific model's results can be fully traced back to the exact data and code that produced it

questions.explanation: Since model behavior depends on both code and the data used to train it, versioning both together supports reproducibility, auditability and rollback if a problem is found later.

questions.question: What could a build or training pipeline failure in continuous integration reveal about an ML project?

options.A: That the project should be abandoned permanently with no further investigation
options.B: That the entire concept of machine learning is fundamentally flawed for the given task
options.C: A defect in code, configuration or new data that broke the pipeline
options.D: That the training data has become completely and irrecoverably corrupted

questions.explanation: A CI failure is a signal to investigate, much like in conventional software, and often points to a specific, fixable issue in code, configuration or a recent data change rather than a fundamental flaw.

questions.question: Why is it useful to include a smoke test of the ML pipeline that runs on a very small subset of data?

options.A: It is required to satisfy a legal certification for AI systems in every jurisdiction
options.B: Fast feedback on whether the pipeline works before a costly full run
options.C: It always produces a fully accurate final model using just the small subset
options.D: It replaces the need to ever evaluate the model on the complete dataset

questions.explanation: A fast, lightweight smoke test on a small sample catches basic pipeline breakages quickly, saving the time and cost of discovering the same problem only after a long full-scale run.

questions.question: What does testing the reproducibility of experiment tracking and logging support in an ML project?

options.A: Eliminating the need for any human data scientist to review experiment results
options.B: Tracing which experiment, data version and settings produced a model
options.C: Permanently deleting the results of any experiment that did not succeed
options.D: Automatically guaranteeing that every experiment achieves state-of-the-art accuracy

questions.explanation: Good experiment tracking, when itself verified to work correctly, lets a team reliably trace a deployed model's lineage back to the exact experiment, data and settings that produced it.

questions.question: Why should unit-level checks be applied to individual data-preprocessing functions in an ML pipeline?

options.A: Because preprocessing functions are always identical across every ML project
options.B: Because unit testing is only ever relevant for the model's final prediction output
options.C: Catching a transformation bug near its source before it spreads
options.D: Because preprocessing functions can never contain any kind of defect

questions.explanation: Testing preprocessing steps individually, such as a normalization or encoding function, catches localized bugs early, before they silently corrupt the data a model is trained on.

questions.question: What risk does verifying the determinism of a training run, given a fixed random seed, help manage?

options.A: The risk that the model will run too quickly during the training process
options.B: The risk that training will require significantly more electrical power than usual
options.C: The risk that a fixed random seed makes a model change its predictions randomly
options.D: The risk that unexplained variation between runs makes debugging and comparison unreliable

questions.explanation: Confirming that a fixed seed produces consistent results helps ensure that observed differences between runs reflect real changes, such as code or data changes, rather than uncontrolled randomness.

questions.question: Why might a code review of a data-loading script specifically check for accidental use of test data during training?

options.A: To ensure the script uses the maximum possible number of lines of code
options.B: To make sure the script produces colorful and visually appealing console output
options.C: To confirm the script was written by the most senior developer on the team
options.D: To prevent data leakage, which would give an unrealistically optimistic performance estimate

questions.explanation: If test data accidentally leaks into training, the model may appear to perform very well while actually failing to generalize, so guarding against this is a specific and valuable review focus.

questions.question: What is the purpose of tracking dependency versions, such as specific library and framework versions, for an ML project?

options.A: To ensure training and inference can be reliably reproduced across different environments and times
options.B: To make sure that only the newest possible version of every library is ever used
options.C: To automatically improve the accuracy of the trained model without any other changes
options.D: To eliminate the need for any further testing of the model once versions are pinned

questions.explanation: Different library versions can subtly change numerical behavior or even results, so tracking and pinning dependencies supports consistent, reproducible training and inference over time.

questions.question: Why might a team add an automated check that fails a build if training loss does not decrease over a small number of epochs on a toy dataset?

options.A: To quickly catch a badly misconfigured run before a costly full one
options.B: Because such a check replaces the need to ever evaluate the model on real data
options.C: Because a training loss that fails to decrease always indicates a hardware failure
options.D: Because this check guarantees the final, fully trained model will never overfit

questions.explanation: A quick sanity check that loss is trending down on a small dataset is a cheap way to catch a badly misconfigured training run early, before investing in a full, expensive training job.

questions.question: What is a chatbot that uses natural language processing to understand and respond to text an example of?

options.A: An AI application in the area of natural language processing
options.B: A database management system with no AI component
options.C: A purely mechanical device with no software component at all
options.D: A network router used to direct internet traffic between servers

questions.explanation: Understanding and generating natural language is a classic AI application area, distinct from purely mechanical devices or conventional networking and database infrastructure.

questions.question: Which AI area is primarily concerned with enabling computers to interpret and understand digital images and video?

options.A: Natural language processing
options.B: Speech synthesis
options.C: Computer vision
options.D: Symbolic logic programming

questions.explanation: Computer vision focuses on extracting meaningful information from visual inputs such as images and video, distinct from language-focused or audio-focused AI areas.

questions.question: A spam filter that was manually coded with fixed keyword rules is replaced by one that learns to recognize spam patterns from thousands of labeled emails. What kind of shift does this represent?

options.A: A shift from a rule-based approach to a machine-learning approach
options.B: A shift that has no meaningful bearing on how the filter should be tested
options.C: A shift from a discriminative model to a purely generative one
options.D: A shift from supervised learning to reinforcement learning

questions.explanation: Moving from hand-coded rules to learning from labeled examples is exactly the shift from rule-based to machine-learning software, which changes the testing focus toward data and statistical behavior.

questions.question: Why might an AI-based system's behavior be harder to fully predict than that of conventional software?

options.A: Its behavior emerges from patterns learned from data rather than from a fixed set of explicit rules
options.B: AI-based systems are exclusively used in situations with no real users at all
options.C: AI-based systems are always physically larger than any conventional software system
options.D: AI-based systems never process any numeric data of any kind

questions.explanation: Because ML-derived behavior comes from learned patterns rather than a fully specified rule set, edge cases can be harder to anticipate in advance compared with conventionally coded logic.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an AI agent, in the sense of an autonomous, goal-directed AI-based component?

options.A: A static webpage that displays the same unchanging text to every visitor
options.B: A software assistant that can plan and execute a multi-step task
options.C: A spreadsheet cell containing a single, simple arithmetic formula
options.D: A printer that prints a document exactly as it was submitted by a user

questions.explanation: An AI agent typically perceives its environment, plans, and takes actions toward a goal with some autonomy, which distinguishes it from the other, purely static or passive examples listed.

questions.question: What best describes "narrow AI"?

options.A: AI with fully general, human-like intelligence across every conceivable domain
options.B: AI designed and trained to perform one specific task or a limited set of related tasks well
options.C: AI that can only be run on very small, narrow physical computer chips
options.D: AI that is restricted by law to processing only numeric input data

questions.explanation: Narrow AI is the kind of AI in practical use today, excelling at a specific task like translation or image recognition, in contrast to the still-hypothetical broad capability of general AI.

questions.question: Which of the following technologies is commonly used to build modern deep-learning-based AI systems?

options.A: Manually punched cards used for programming instructions
options.B: Analog vacuum-tube circuitry from early computing history
options.C: Artificial neural networks
options.D: Simple flat-file text storage with no computation involved

questions.explanation: Neural networks, especially deep architectures with many layers, underlie most modern high-performing AI systems for tasks like vision and language, unlike the outdated or unrelated options listed.

questions.question: What does "fairness" mean as a quality characteristic for an AI-based system?

options.A: The system's user interface uses the same font size on every single screen
options.B: The system does not produce systematically unjustified different outcomes for different groups
options.C: The system is legally required to be free of charge for every user
options.D: The system always produces exactly identical numeric output for every possible input

questions.explanation: Fairness concerns avoiding unjustified disparate treatment or impact across groups defined by attributes such as gender or ethnicity, which is a key quality concern for many AI applications.

questions.question: Why is "safety" often highlighted as a particularly important quality characteristic for certain AI-based systems, such as autonomous vehicles?

options.A: Failures in these systems can directly cause physical harm to people or property
options.B: Safety characteristics are identical in importance for every kind of software system
options.C: Safety is a concept that applies only to systems with no machine learning component
options.D: Safety only matters for AI systems that have absolutely no users at all

questions.explanation: In domains like autonomous driving or medical devices, an AI failure can have direct, serious physical consequences, which is why safety receives particular emphasis in those contexts.

questions.question: What does "security" mean as a quality characteristic specifically relevant to AI-based systems?

options.A: Protection against adversarial attacks, poisoning and model theft
options.B: The physical strength of the building housing the training servers
options.C: The number of passwords required to log into the training environment
options.D: The color scheme chosen for a security dashboard's user interface

questions.explanation: AI-specific security concerns extend beyond conventional cybersecurity to include threats unique to ML systems, such as adversarial inputs, data poisoning, and extraction of a model's parameters or training data.

questions.question: Why might "reliability" of an AI-based system be assessed differently than for conventional software?

options.A: AI-based systems are always inherently perfectly reliable by their very nature
options.B: Reliability is a concept that has no meaning at all for any AI-based system
options.C: Reliability for AI systems can only ever be assessed by end users, never by testers
options.D: Statistical performance measures may be needed alongside uptime

questions.explanation: Beyond conventional reliability measures like uptime, an AI system's reliability often also involves the statistical consistency and expected accuracy of its predictions across intended conditions.

questions.question: Which pair of AI quality characteristics is commonly cited as being in tension, requiring a deliberate trade-off?

options.A: Compatibility and usability, which never conflict in any AI system
options.B: Accuracy and interpretability, since some highly accurate models are also the hardest to explain
options.C: Portability and installability, which are always perfectly aligned with no trade-off
options.D: Maintainability and testability, which are always identical in every respect

questions.explanation: Complex models, such as deep neural networks, often achieve high accuracy but are hard to interpret, while simpler, more interpretable models may sacrifice some accuracy, a commonly cited trade-off.

questions.question: Why is "usability" still a relevant quality characteristic for AI-based systems, even when the AI component itself works correctly?

options.A: Users still need to understand and effectively interact with the system's AI-driven outputs
options.B: Usability testing becomes entirely unnecessary once a model reaches high accuracy
options.C: Usability only ever applies to software systems that contain no AI components
options.D: A correctly functioning AI component automatically guarantees good usability

questions.explanation: Even a highly accurate model needs to present its outputs, such as recommendations or explanations, in a way users can actually understand and act on, so usability remains a distinct concern.

questions.question: What is a "quality characteristic" in the sense used by standards like ISO/IEC 25010 and its AI extension ISO/IEC 25059?

options.A: A category, like reliability, used to organize aspects of quality
options.B: A legal document required before any software product may be sold
options.C: A physical component installed inside a computer's central processing unit
options.D: A single specific numeric metric with one universally agreed correct target value

questions.explanation: Quality characteristics are the organizing categories, like performance efficiency or security, under which more specific quality concerns and measurable attributes are grouped.

questions.question: A pretrained large language model that is adapted for a company's specific support use case by further training on the company's own data is an example of what?

options.A: Running the base model with absolutely no further training or adaptation
options.B: Manually hand-coding every possible support response as a fixed rule
options.C: Deleting the model entirely and starting a new project from nothing
options.D: Fine-tuning a pretrained model

questions.explanation: Fine-tuning takes a model already trained on general data and continues training it on domain-specific data, adapting it to the target use case without starting from scratch.

questions.question: How does retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improve an LLM's answers?

options.A: By preventing the LLM from ever accessing any external information whatsoever
options.B: By deleting all of the LLM's own internal, pretrained knowledge before answering
options.C: By requiring the LLM to be completely retrained from scratch for every single question
options.D: By retrieving relevant external documents and providing them as context alongside the prompt

questions.explanation: RAG supplies the model with relevant retrieved context at inference time, which can improve accuracy and reduce fabricated answers compared with relying solely on the model's trained-in knowledge.

questions.question: In a large language model, what does raising the "temperature" parameter tend to do?

options.A: Decrease the total number of tokens the model is able to process
options.B: Guarantee that the model's output becomes completely and perfectly accurate
options.C: Increase the physical temperature of the server hardware running the model
options.D: Increase the randomness and diversity of the generated output

questions.explanation: Temperature controls sampling randomness during generation; higher values produce more varied, less predictable output, while lower values make output more focused and deterministic.

questions.question: What does k-fold cross-validation help assess about a model, compared with a single train-test split?

options.A: The programming language originally used to implement the model
options.B: The physical amount of disk storage the trained model file occupies
options.C: The exact number of parameters contained within the trained model
options.D: A more robust estimate by averaging results across several splits

questions.explanation: By training and evaluating across several different splits of the data, k-fold cross-validation reduces the risk that a single lucky or unlucky split gives a misleading performance estimate.

questions.question: What is a "baseline model" used for during ML development?

options.A: A simple reference point to judge if a complex model is worth its cost
options.B: Serving as the only model that will ever be deployed to production
options.C: Storing the raw, completely unprocessed training data before it is used
options.D: Replacing the need to evaluate any more sophisticated model at all

questions.explanation: A simple baseline, such as always predicting the most common class, sets a floor that a more sophisticated model should clearly beat to justify its added complexity.

questions.question: Why is defining precise expected results often harder for AI-based systems than for conventional software?

options.A: Conventional software is defined as never having any expected results at all
options.B: AI-based systems never accept any form of numeric input from a user
options.C: Defining expected results is impossible for absolutely every kind of software system
options.D: Correct behavior may not have one single, universally agreed answer

questions.explanation: Tasks such as summarization or open-ended generation often admit multiple reasonable outputs, unlike a conventional calculation with one deterministically correct answer, which makes the oracle problem especially relevant.

questions.question: Why might testers deliberately run the same AI-based test case multiple times rather than just once?

options.A: Because a single test execution is always technically impossible for any AI system
options.B: Because running a test more than once always makes the underlying model more accurate
options.C: To account for non-deterministic behavior and observe the range or consistency of outputs
options.D: Because repeated execution eliminates the need to ever define any expected result

questions.explanation: Since many AI systems can produce different outputs on different runs for the same input, repeating a test helps reveal the actual range and consistency of behavior, not just one sample of it.

questions.question: Why might testers specifically evaluate the "explanations" a system provides for its AI-driven decisions, not just the decisions themselves?

options.A: Because explanations are always guaranteed to be completely correct by design
options.B: Because testing explanations removes the need to ever test the decision output itself
options.C: To check that the explanation is actually accurate and genuinely reflects the real reasoning
options.D: Because explanations can only ever exist for systems that produce no numeric output

questions.explanation: An explanation could be plausible-sounding but not actually reflect the real factors that drove a decision, so verifying the explanation's genuine accuracy is itself a distinct testing concern.

questions.question: Why is verifying label quality important as part of testing an AI-based system's inputs?

options.A: Label quality only ever matters for systems that use absolutely no training data
options.B: Label quality checks are exclusively relevant to systems that generate images
options.C: Incorrect labels can directly mislead what the model learns and how it eventually performs
options.D: Verifying labels always guarantees that the resulting trained model will be perfectly accurate

questions.explanation: Since supervised learning depends on labels as ground truth, verifying their correctness is a foundational check to prevent mistaken patterns from being learned by the model.

questions.question: Why should testers check for missing values in a dataset intended for training an ML model?

options.A: Missing values always automatically improve the resulting model's final accuracy
options.B: Checking for missing values is only ever relevant to non-numeric text data
options.C: Missing values can bias training or require handling that affects behavior
options.D: Missing values are impossible to occur in any dataset by their very definition

questions.explanation: Missing data can distort statistics, break processing steps, or require imputation choices that themselves affect the trained model, so checking for and handling them appropriately matters.

questions.question: After deploying a new model version, a tester first sends one simple, known input just to confirm the service responds at all before running the full evaluation suite. What kind of check is this?

options.A: An adversarial robustness assessment using crafted attack inputs
options.B: A fairness audit comparing performance across demographic subgroups
options.C: A smoke test, a fast sanity check before deeper testing is invested
options.D: A full statistical performance evaluation with confidence intervals

questions.explanation: A quick, minimal check that the deployed service is even working is a smoke test, which is meant to catch basic breakage cheaply before committing to a more thorough evaluation.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: Why might testers check for class balance in a classification dataset?

options.A: Class balance only matters for datasets that contain absolutely no labels of any kind
options.B: Severe imbalance between classes can cause the model to under-learn the rarer, minority class
options.C: Class balance is a concept that applies exclusively to regression tasks, not classification
options.D: Checking class balance always guarantees the model will be free of any bias

questions.explanation: When one class vastly outnumbers another, a model can achieve seemingly good overall metrics while performing poorly on the rare class, which is exactly what class balance checks are meant to catch.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: Why should testers check that numeric feature values fall within expected, plausible ranges?

options.A: Numeric ranges are entirely irrelevant to how any ML model actually learns
options.B: Feature values are always guaranteed to be correct and never need any range checking
options.C: An out-of-range value often signals a data problem, not a real one
options.D: Range checks always guarantee that a trained model will achieve perfect accuracy

questions.explanation: A value far outside a plausible range, such as a negative age, often signals an upstream data problem rather than a genuine data point, and such problems can distort what the model learns.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: Why should input data testing verify that a data pipeline correctly handles a data schema change, such as a renamed field?

options.A: Schema changes are always automatically and correctly handled by every data pipeline
options.B: Verifying schema handling is only relevant for systems that use no structured data
options.C: A renamed field can never have any effect on how a machine learning pipeline behaves
options.D: An undetected schema mismatch could silently corrupt or drop data flowing into training or inference

questions.explanation: A pipeline that does not correctly account for a schema change might silently misinterpret or drop data, introducing a subtle failure that could go unnoticed without a specific test for it.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: Why is checking for duplicate records a relevant input-data test for an ML project?

options.A: Duplicate records always improve a model's ability to generalize to genuinely new data
options.B: Checking for duplicates is only relevant to datasets that contain no numeric values
options.C: Duplicate records are impossible to occur in any dataset collected from any real source
options.D: Duplicates can bias training or inflate performance if they cross splits

questions.explanation: Repeated records can skew the effective weight given to certain examples during training, and duplicates leaking across a train and test split can make performance look better than it truly is.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a "test oracle" more broadly in the context of model testing, when one is available?

options.A: Providing the expected or correct result that an actual model output can be compared against
options.B: Providing a random number that has no relationship to the model's actual output
options.C: Providing the marketing materials that will describe the model to end customers
options.D: Providing the physical electricity that powers the servers running the trained model

questions.explanation: A test oracle, whatever its specific form, supplies a basis for judging whether an actual output is correct or acceptable, which is central to deciding pass or fail for any test.

questions.question: Why might testers evaluate a classification model's performance separately for different demographic subgroups?

options.A: Because subgroup evaluation always guarantees identical performance across every group
options.B: To detect if the model performs meaningfully worse for some groups than others, indicating a fairness concern
options.C: Because overall aggregate performance always fully and completely describes subgroup performance
options.D: Because subgroup-level evaluation is only relevant for models that use no personal data whatsoever

questions.explanation: An overall average metric can hide meaningfully worse performance for a specific subgroup, so disaggregated evaluation is often necessary to detect and address such fairness issues.

questions.question: What does testing a model's "latency" typically measure?

options.A: The time taken for the model to produce a prediction after receiving an input
options.B: The number of engineers who contributed code to the model's training pipeline
options.C: The number of distinct classes the model is able to predict
options.D: The total physical file size of the model on disk in megabytes

questions.explanation: Latency measures response time, which matters for user experience and for systems with real-time requirements, distinct from concerns like model size or classification granularity.

questions.question: Why might testers deliberately evaluate a model's behavior on inputs that are unlike anything in its training data (out-of-distribution inputs)?

options.A: Because a model is always guaranteed to behave identically on any kind of input
options.B: Because testing on unfamiliar inputs removes the need to ever test on familiar ones
options.C: Because out-of-distribution inputs are impossible to construct for any real system
options.D: To see how it behaves on genuinely unfamiliar situations

questions.explanation: Real-world deployment inevitably exposes a model to inputs unlike its training data, so deliberately testing this scenario reveals whether the model degrades gracefully or fails unpredictably.
